triples.evidence: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!

triples.subject: Will DePue
triples.evidence: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated;

triples.subject: Nvidia
triples.evidence: A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon. The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public. “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says. Huang resigned on Thursday , four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs . Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding .

triples.subject: Anthropic
triples.evidence: Anthropic's Claude for Manufacturing plugs AI directly into factory software to automate industrial workflows。

triples.subject: Anthropic
triples.evidence: Anthropic has released Claude for Manufacturing, a plugin giving the AI direct access to industrial software to automate factory workflows. The new solution connects via four universal interfaces to Autodesk Fusion, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft 365, and Infor. Other systems can be integrated through file exports to Microsoft 365. With 17 specific skills , the AI drafts quotes from actual inventory, compares suppliers, generates quality reports and design variants, and analyzes sensor data and manuals during machine downtime. Via an added Infor plugin, Claude can also order from backup suppliers when deliveries are delayed and reschedule production—after human approval. All results are linked to original source documents for employee review before reaching customers or suppliers. The plugin is available to Team and Enterprise customers but doesn't control physical machines yet. For that, Anthropic is separately developing the Model Hardware Standard as a research preview, connecting AI agents to devices like robotic arms and microscopes via standardized drivers. This cuts setup time from weeks or months to hours or minutes but still requires human oversight due to the AI's limited grasp of physical processes.

triples.subject: Joby Aviation
triples.evidence: along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms. None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls. According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?

triples.subject: Palantir
triples.evidence: it’ll occupy a more modest, behind-the-scenes role. Already, data companies like Palantir and aviation industry stalwarts like Jeppesen and Thales are selling AI-enabled software that lets regulators, airlines, and flight dispatchers sift through masses of data to identify risks and plan aircraft and crew scheduling. In September, the FAA announced that it deployed software built by the Boston-based data company Air Space Intelligence. The new AI-powered tool is called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” or SMART, and it’s aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” The program isn’t intended to replace controllers, the government says, but to make doing their jobs easier by using predictive AI to head off scheduling snags. “Combining SMART with our ongoing hardware upgrades gives us the tools to cut flight delays, optimize traffic, and keep airspace capacity across the country open—all while maintaining our gold standard of safety,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said in a press release . Joby Aviation’s S4 electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Photograph: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images The system is supposed to help controllers make decisions, not make those decisions for them. But if the program feeds nonsensical information into the system, will human operators be able to catch the mistake?

triples.subject: LangChain
triples.evidence: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation。

triples.subject: LangChain
triples.evidence: Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday. That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP. LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence. With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use. True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.
